opus-5.5.text:
Well, first I should say I can't speak for OpenAI's actual product plans. I can only share how I think about it as a researcher who works on reinforcement learning and agents.

I think of it in a few stages. Right now most agents are still what I'd call "you ask, it does." You give it a task, like searching for something, writing some code, or filling out a form, and it runs for a few minutes and comes back. That's useful, but it's still essentially a better tool. The human is still the one who decides what to do, breaks the problem down, and checks the result.

The next form, which I think we're starting to see, is the agent that runs for much longer, hours or even days, on something fairly open-ended. Think of a research assistant that keeps working on a problem, or a coding agent that owns a whole feature rather than one function. The key technical problem there isn't really intelligence in a single step. It's long-horizon reliability: can it plan, notice when it's going wrong, recover, and know when to come back and ask you? That's very much a reinforcement learning problem, because you need to train on the outcome of long trajectories, not just imitate good single responses.

Then the form I find most interesting is when the agent becomes proactive, more like a colleague than a tool. It understands your context and your goals, and sometimes it comes to you and says, "I noticed this, should I handle it?" That changes the product from a chat box into something closer to a team member. Once you have that, you naturally get multi-agent setups, where one person manages several agents, and the agents coordinate with each other.

I don't think the final form is one super app that does everything. More likely there's a general foundation model with strong agentic ability underneath, and many different interfaces on top: in your browser, your IDE, your phone, your company's workflow. The interface matters less over time. What matters is whether you trust it enough to delegate.

So for me the real question isn't which product shape wins. It's when trust crosses a threshold, when people are comfortable letting an agent act for them without watching every step. That depends on capability, but also on safety, on how well the agent understands what you actually want, and on whether it knows the limits of its own ability. Whoever solves that, whether OpenAI or anyone else, will define what the agent product looks like.

r001.rationale: The response describes multiple possible interfaces—browser, IDE, phone, and company workflows—but does not clearly state that UI agents are only one possible product form.

fable-5.1.text:
I think there are basically three layers, and OpenAI will probably end up doing all of them at once rather than picking one.

The first layer is the thing that's already here: ChatGPT itself becoming the agent. Right now people still think of it as a chat window, but the real shift is that the model starts taking actions on your behalf: browsing, running code, filling out forms, operating a computer. Operator and the deep research style products are early versions of that. The product form there is simple: you describe a goal, you walk away, and you come back to a finished result instead of a conversation. The interface stays conversational, but the unit of work changes from a message to a task.

The second layer is the agent as a platform. OpenAI can't build every vertical application themselves, so they'll expose the agent capability through APIs, tool calling, and some kind of app or GPTs ecosystem, and let developers build agents for specific domains: coding, customer service, finance, legal. In that form the product isn't really a consumer-facing thing, it's more like an operating system for agents. Whoever controls the model, the memory layer, and the tool integration layer gets a lot of leverage, which is why that fight matters so much.

The third layer is the one I find most interesting from a research perspective, which is the personal agent that lives with you over a long time. It knows your context, your preferences, your history, and it coordinates across your email, your calendar, your devices. That requires solving long-horizon memory and reliability problems that are still genuinely hard. If an agent is going to act for you for weeks or months, a two or three percent error rate on each step compounds into something unacceptable. So the product form there is constrained by the research: you'll probably see narrow but reliable agents first, and the fully general assistant later.

If I had to bet on the sequencing, I'd say coding agents first, because the feedback is verifiable and developers tolerate rough edges. Then research and knowledge work agents. Then the consumer personal agent last, maybe tied to hardware, because that's where reliability and trust requirements are highest.

r001.rationale: The response presents ChatGPT acting through a conversational interface as the first of three agent product forms, alongside an agent platform and a long-term personal agent.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a few possible forms. One is an agent inside ChatGPT: you give it a goal, and instead of just answering, it carries out a sequence of actions and comes back with a result. Another is an agent embedded in the tools people already use, where it has access to the context and can help complete a particular workflow. And a third is a platform that lets developers build agents for different industries and tasks.

The interesting question is how much responsibility the user can hand over. Answering a question is one thing; doing something that takes an hour, involves several applications, and requires judgment is quite different. The product needs to make it clear when the agent can proceed, when it should ask you, and how you can check what it did.

So my guess is that the first useful products will have fairly well-defined tasks and clear ways to verify the outcome. As reliability improves, those boundaries can expand. I wouldn’t assume the final form is simply a chat window, but conversation is a natural starting point for telling an agent what you want.

r001.rationale: The response presents an agent inside ChatGPT as one possible form, alongside agents embedded in existing tools and a developer platform.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a few possible forms. One is an assistant inside a conversational interface: you give it a goal, and it works through the steps for you. Another is an agent embedded in the software you already use, with enough context to help you complete a specific workflow. A third is something that runs in the background and comes back when it has a result or needs your decision.

I don’t know which direction OpenAI will prioritize. But the important shift is from answering a question to completing a task. That changes the product requirements: users need to understand what the agent can do, what access it has, and when it will ask for confirmation. The interface may still look like a chat window, but the real product is whether you can reliably delegate work to it.

r001.rationale: The response describes several possible forms, including a conversational-interface assistant, an agent embedded in existing software, and a background agent. This communicates that UI agents are one possible form among others.
